title: doxa
summary: These passages portray divine glory through vision, presence, transformation, and light. In Exodus 33, Moses asks to see God’s glory and receives only a limited disclosure; Isaiah 6 depicts a vision of the Lord whose glory fills the earth. John 1 speaks of the Word’s glory made visible; 2 Corinthians 3 contrasts fading glory with a lasting transformation; Revelation 21 pictures God’s glory illuminating the renewed city. The references include Hebrew and Greek texts with related imagery, not one identical lexical use.
historical_context: The set includes a narrative exchange with Moses, Isaiah’s prophetic vision, a Gospel prologue, Paul’s argument about Moses and transformation, and Revelation’s city vision. These settings come from the biblical texts; no external history of the term or ancient comparison is added.
canonical_context: Exodus and Isaiah depict divine glory in encounters and visions. John connects glory with the Word; Paul relates glory to the reading of Moses and transformation; Revelation pictures God’s glory as the light of the renewed city. These passages trace a theme across genres without implying that the Hebrew and Greek terms have identical ranges.
literary_context: Exodus narrates a request and partial revelation, Isaiah recounts a vision, John opens with a theological prologue, Paul reasons through a scriptural contrast, and Revelation uses visionary imagery. The forms show glory as something requested, seen, reflected, and anticipated.
covenantal_significance: The passages connect God’s presence with revelation, transformation, and hope. Moses is not granted an unrestricted sight of God; Isaiah’s vision leads to a prophetic commission; Paul describes transformation; Revelation imagines a city illuminated by God’s glory. Each text adds a distinct dimension.
canonical_role: This entry gathers biblical portrayals of divine glory in narrative, prophetic vision, Gospel reflection, apostolic argument, and apocalyptic hope. It helps readers follow the theme without treating related translations as proof of one identical original-language usage.
